title: Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction
author: Philip E. Tetlock, Dan Gardner
thesisParagraph: Most confident-sounding forecasts are untested performances. Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner tracked expert predictions over decades and found that prestige, fluency, and decisiveness routinely masquerade as forecasting skill. The book then identifies a small group of people — superforecasters — who outperform not by genius but by disciplined habits: breaking problems into estimable parts, anchoring on base rates before adjusting for inside information, expressing uncertainty as calibrated probabilities, updating proportionately to new evidence, seeking feedback, and staying open to revision. The argument is not that the future is controllable. It is that better-calibrated thinking consistently beats overconfident punditry, and that the habits behind it can be learned.

coreIdeas.name: Prestige is not track record
coreIdeas.oneSentence: The credibility signals we trust most — fame, authority, decisiveness — are almost entirely uncorrelated with forecasting accuracy.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Separate how confident a source sounds from how accurate it has actually been over time.

coreIdeas.name: Illusions of understanding
coreIdeas.oneSentence: A coherent explanation feels like knowledge before the evidence has earned that confidence.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Catch the moment your explanation stops feeling like a hypothesis and starts feeling like a verdict.

coreIdeas.name: Scorekeeping makes improvement possible
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Vague probability language cannot be checked; a specific number can.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Translate hedge words into percentages so your claims can meet outcomes later.

coreIdeas.name: Question substitution
coreIdeas.oneSentence: The hardest part of forecasting is staying on the hard question instead of sliding to an easier proxy.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Ask what you are actually trying to predict and resist the pull toward the question that feels answerable.

coreIdeas.name: Fermi decomposition plus outside view
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Break the problem into parts small enough to estimate, then check each part against base rates before adjusting for inside information.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Decompose the question, look up the reference class, and only then apply what you know specifically.

coreIdeas.name: Calibrated probability expression
coreIdeas.oneSentence: A forecast that acknowledges its own uncertainty is more honest and more useful than one that claims false precision.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: State a probability range that reflects what you actually know, distinguishing what more evidence could resolve from what remains irreducibly uncertain.

coreIdeas.name: Proportionate updating
coreIdeas.oneSentence: The size of a revision should match the strength of the new signal, not the emotional salience of the news.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Before adjusting your estimate, ask how much this piece of information should actually move it.

coreIdeas.name: Perpetual beta
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Forecasting skill compounds only when you treat each mistake as auditable evidence rather than a reputation to manage.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Keep a record precise enough to check and stay open to correction that can still hurt.

coreIdeas.name: Superteams preserve disagreement
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Collective forecasting beats individual forecasting only when dissent is kept alive long enough to improve the shared estimate.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Voice the reservation before the group settles, not after the cost of being wrong arrives.

coreIdeas.name: Decisive humility
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Strong leadership and strong forecasting are compatible only when action is decoupled from the pretense of certainty.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Commit to a course while building structures that keep local judgment alive after the decision.

coreIdeas.name: Forecasting limits and planning for surprise
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Accepting what forecasting cannot do clarifies what it can do — and that boundary is itself a forecasting insight.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Distinguish tractable uncertainty from genuine black swans, then prepare conditionally for the latter instead of ignoring it.

coreIdeas.name: Institutional scorekeeping
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Forecasting improves at scale only when institutions demand outcome scores and reward accuracy over persuasiveness.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Demand that predictions meet outcomes publicly before granting the forecaster authority on the next question.

targetReader: Managers, analysts, policy thinkers, and anyone who makes decisions under uncertainty and suspects their confident gut is not as reliable as it feels.

signatureMoves: uses fox-versus-hedgehog contrast, calibration, base rates, and updating
keeps claims probabilistic and allergic to pundit certainty
turns forecasting into scored habits rather than genius
sounds empirical, modest, and exacting about evidence quality
avoidMoves: Avoid "The point is" as a paragraph hinge.
Avoid "the question is" as a setup crutch.
Avoid triadic abstract-noun lists such as clarity, courage, and resilience.
Do not let confidence outrun track record.
Do not make uncertainty sound like indecision.

voiceSpecimens: A prediction without a probability is still wearing costume jewelry.
Update early, score honestly, and let the fox stay restless.
voiceAntiSpecimens: In this chapter, we will explore the fascinating world of probabilistic thinking and what it means for modern decision-making.
By applying these groundbreaking insights, you can transform the way you approach uncertainty.
Experts often get it wrong, and that is why you need to think differently about the future.
The key takeaway here is that calibration is absolutely essential to becoming a better thinker.
This powerful research shows us that even ordinary people can achieve extraordinary forecasting results.
teachingArc: The book opens by showing that the forecasting ecosystem is broken in a specific way: credibility signals (fame, authority, fluency) crowd out accuracy signals (track record, calibration, revision). It then goes looking for people who actually forecast well and asks what they do. The middle chapters dissect each ingredient: decomposition, probability expression, update discipline, feedback hunger, and team structure. The final chapters stress-test the claim by asking what forecasting genuinely cannot do, then close by arguing that the same discipline applied to institutions could change what gets rewarded in public life.
forbiddenMoves: Treating 'be humble' as the lesson — the book teaches specific calibration mechanics, not generic modesty
Confusing update frequency with update quality — more news consumption is not the variable
Using the word 'probably' in examples without attaching a number — every hedge word in this book demands a percentage
Treating superforecasters as geniuses or special talents — the book explicitly rejects that frame
Letting 'black swan' become an excuse to dismiss all forecasting — the book defends careful prediction while accepting limits
Collapsing epistemic and aleatory uncertainty into one vague 'things are uncertain' gesture
Do not make predictions without probabilities.
Do not praise expertise without feedback and calibration.
